items.q: Where does most background radiation come from?
items.correct: Mostly natural sources — radon gas, rocks, cosmic rays and food; only a little is man-made.
items.misconception: Almost entirely from nuclear power stations.
items.random_wrong: There is no background radiation in everyday life.
items.why: The biggest contributor is usually radon gas from the ground. Nuclear power contributes only a tiny fraction of the dose.

items.q: Do all atoms of the same element have the same number of neutrons?
items.correct: No — isotopes are atoms of one element with the same protons but different numbers of neutrons.
items.misconception: Yes, every atom of an element is identical with the same neutrons.
items.random_wrong: Isotopes have different numbers of protons.
items.why: An element is fixed by its proton (atomic) number; neutron number can vary, giving isotopes such as carbon-12 and carbon-14.

items.q: What must balance in a nuclear decay equation?
items.correct: Both the mass numbers and the atomic (proton) numbers must balance on each side.
items.misconception: Only the mass numbers need to balance.
items.random_wrong: Nuclear equations don't have to obey conservation rules.
items.why: Nucleon number and charge are conserved: the totals of the top numbers (mass) and bottom numbers (charge) are equal before and after the decay.
